baer-heitev/1:א: In his hand. And if they transferred it to the non-Jew through kinyan or via land, even though they did not deliver it to him until after Pesach, if it is not on the Jew's responsibility it is permitted. Shach.
baer-heitev/1:ב: From now. And if he did not lend him money but only said to him: if I do not do a certain matter, the chametz shall be yours from now — it is forbidden, for it is asmakhta (and according to Raavad there is no law of asmakhta with a non-Jew). And know that if one of these matters is lacking it is forbidden — meaning it is forbidden for any Jew to derive benefit from that chametz even though it is in a non-Jew's hand; and it requires study whether if he did not say to him from now he is obligated to redeem it from the non-Jew and destroy it, for otherwise he pays his debt from prohibited benefit. Magen Avraham. And Chayei Adam wrote one should be stringent to redeem it — see there. And if it is still in the Jew's hand only that he pledged it to the non-Jew, it is obvious it is forbidden to give it to him.
baer-heitev/1:ג: Permitted. And if at the time of the loan he intends to redeem it after Pesach, it is certainly forbidden, for it is like hiding it in the non-Jew's hand. Taz — see there.
baer-heitev/2:_: Forbidden. It appears to me that on Pesach the Jew is not obligated to destroy it, for it is still in the non-Jew's possession since perhaps he will redeem it; and even if the non-Jew came on Pesach and gave its value, it is permitted to let the non-Jew take it. Magen Avraham and Kaf HaChayim disagree — see there. And a Jew who takes a pledge from his fellow who lent him transgresses, for a Jew does not acquire a pledge from his fellow without from now. Magen Avraham. And Taz in siman 443 s.k. 4 wrote the borrower is obligated to destroy.
beer-hagolah/1:א: Mishnah Pesachim 31a, established according to Rava, not all agreements of the poskim.
beer-hagolah/1:ב: Tur in the name of Raavad and Rosh, and likewise Ran.
beur-hagra/1:א: (1) And he pledged it. There regarding that he left it as pledge with him etc. — the objection that he said to him etc. implies it refers to leaving as pledge; and likewise in the baraita: a Jew who left as pledge etc. and if etc. — see Magen Avraham.
beur-hagra/1:ב: Even if the time did not arrive etc. — for otherwise Rava would not have challenged from the Mishnah, and from now would not be needed. And not like Rambam and R' Efraim who wrote specifically when the time arrived before Pesach, and they inferred from the Tosefta; and see Rosh. Nevertheless, that which is written even etc. implies that also when the time arrived before Pesach one must say from now, and the reason is asmakhta as written in chapter Eizehu Neshech 66:1–2. And for Nemyonim the Mishnah is difficult; but in truth that he said to him etc., and Magen Avraham wrote: although Rambam's view is there is no asmakhta in a pledge, here a Jew from a non-Jew does not acquire etc. And the explanation is Rambam wrote in chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechirah and in Shulchan Aruch Choshen Mishpat siman 207 seif 11 that in a deposit when he forgives you there is no asmakhta; and see Ran in Nedarim 27b s.v. she'ani heinah that said etc. nevertheless here a Jew from a non-Jew etc. And at first glance his words require study, for a Jew from a non-Jew does not acquire before collection — but why not acquire at its time? And one can say they challenged him from that in Bava Metzia cited above that specifically when he said from now; and one can explain this case is different — a movable pledge that he acquired for her; and see Tosafot there 67b s.v. shevi'it etc., and this is what he said here a Jew etc. But he wrote there in chapter 11 one who transfers whether land etc., and likewise Shulchan Aruch there seif 11 — if so that answer is void; and see there Magen Avraham, and several answers are possible. But Raavad's view here is before Pesach one need not from now, for there is no asmakhta with a non-Jew, and only after Pesach one needs from now; and his proof from what the Tosefta says before Pesach — therefore one must say as Ran wrote that the Tosefta deals when he did not say from now; and see Magen Avraham there, for it appears from his words they did not agree with him on the first law. And he holds even with a non-Jew one needs from now; and it appears the reason is they explain what the Tosefta says before Pesach refers to when he said to him, as Rosh wrote. But Raavad's words are primary, and there is no necessity in the geonim's words to contradict him, for they only wrote the Gemara's law after Pesach. And see what we wrote in Choshen Mishpat siman 207 seif 2 that Rambam's view is not as in the case of one who acquired with one [statement] etc., that what is in his hand is not asmakhta whether land or movable property, as Magen Avraham wrote — rather another reason in a matter that depends whether he acquires for him immediately, which is like saying to him from now, which is not so when he says if; and as Rav Hai Gaon wrote. And that which is written therefore one who gives a deposit refers only to the latter clause if the seller retracted; and this is what is written there, and likewise one who paid etc., and likewise all conditions etc., that whoever says if it will be etc. — all implies asmakhta that he did not acquire; therefore Rambam's words and Shulchan Aruch here are correct.
beur-hagra/1:ג: If he pledged it etc. and said to him. There, only the common case such as etc.; but a Jew who lent etc. But if he did not pledge it, even though he said to him from now the Jew does not acquire since they did not acquire from him through kinyan; and see Magen Avraham s.k. 5: even if there is not etc. and there is not etc. Tosafot s.v. shekoneh etc., and the whole sugya etc.
biur-halacha/1:_: And he pledged it in his hand — see Mishna Berurah regarding if they transferred through kinyan: we wrote to be lenient in the name of several acharonim, and they wrote some are stringent, and this is in Peri Megadim; and there is concern for Rama's view in Choshen Mishpat siman 207 seif 14 that from now does not remove asmakhta without an important court unless it was tevoi yadai and from now, as Semag wrote s.k. 18 — see there. But in truth it is not proven there at all that tevoi yadai is required; only that it must be in the manner of a loan and that he did him a favor, as explained in Tosafot 66 and Rosh, and likewise in Piskei Tosafot; if so, the same applies here, for it was in the manner of a loan and he pledged his pledge to him even though it still rests in his possession — unless one holds that here it is worse because it rests in the borrower's possession; requires study.
biur-halacha/2:א: Forbidden — see Mishna Berurah in what we wrote that he is obligated to destroy it before Pesach, and this is the view of all the acharonim, not like Magen Avraham; and see Mekor Chayim and Bigdei Yesha and Yad Ephraim, who wrote to uphold Magen Avraham's words. And the content of their words is nearly one: there is no need to destroy and lose the pledge with one's hands and lose his debt; it is better for him to wait until the time the non-Jew set, and perhaps he will pay his debt and redeem his pledge; and if he sees that soon the time will expire and he does not redeem, he may then forgive him the debt and say: I am as though I received payment, and its value as though the non-Jew paid — and the matter is revealed that the pledge belonged to the non-Jew and he did not transgress bal yeira'eh. But perhaps one should be concerned lest he forget to make this arrangement before the time arrives and come to bal yeira'eh; but in truth one should make this arrangement orally [meaning he forgives the debt before a court or before witnesses not in the non-Jew's presence, for that too is mechilah and automatically the pledge is not his; if so, even when the time arrives and he did not redeem, he did not transgress bal yeira'eh and the pledge remains tevoi yadai as Yad Ephraim intended] — and in this manner the chametz will also be permitted to him afterward; but perhaps it is like an evasion, like that in siman 448 seif 5 — see there.
biur-halacha/2:ב: But if he did not say to him — see what Mishna Berurah wrote: per the Mechaber's view, the same applies before Pesach — we need from now; and we inferred this from the Mechaber's language that wrote even, as Magen Avraham and Gra inferred in the seif before this. And it is further proven thus according to Rambam per Rambam that the Mishnah in chapter Kol Shehu and the whole sugya deal before Pesach; if so, when we establish the Mishnah where he said to him from now, the latter clause also refers to a non-Jew who lent a Jew on his chametz. And likewise there specifically when he said from now; otherwise the Jew does not acquire; and likewise proven further from that baraita brought in the Gemara regarding a non-Jew who left as pledge festival bread with a Jew that he does not transgress, and if he said to him I have reached you he transgresses — and they establish it at the outset that he did not say to him from now. And for Rambam it certainly deals before Pesach per Rambam's words; therefore also here if the non-Jew did not say to him from now the Jew does not acquire, because it is asmakhta, and he does not hold like Raavad that there is no asmakhta with a non-Jew. And I saw one of the acharonim who wrote the opposite of this, and it is proven in his words that certainly the other poskim do not disagree with Raavad's reasoning except in the first clause where the Jew left the pledge in the non-Jew's hand — and the reason is that although asmakhta does not apply in non-Jewish law, nevertheless one cannot obligate the Jew and declare his pledge in a gentile's hand forbidden, since in our law it is asmakhta; as we say in general: a Jew and a non-Jew who come to judgment — if you can vindicate him by Jewish law, vindicate him and say such is our law — unlike in the latter clause where the non-Jew left the pledge in the Jew's hand and by their law it is declared when the time arrives and he did not redeem; there the reasoning is reversed, and certainly we follow their law to leave the pledge in the Jew's hand, as we say: if you cannot vindicate by our law, etc.; if so, according to all, even if he did not say to him from now, if the time arrived before Pesach it is declared in the Jew's hand and he transgresses. In my humble opinion it appears as we wrote that it depends on the dispute cited, as proven from Magen Avraham and Gra in the Mechaber's view; and because one can say those who disagree with Raavad — their reason is there is no reason to distinguish here between non-Jew and Jew, for the reason asmakhta does not acquire is because he relies that it will not happen so and therefore does not finalize and acquire [as Gra challenged on this reasoning against Raavad's view]; if so, there is no difference between a Jew borrowing on his pledge and a non-Jew borrowing on his pledge — in both we do not put it in their minds that they will not redeem and they did not finalize and acquire. And what was proven from that we say if you cannot etc. vindicate him — one can say this reasoning does not help to establish it in his possession except from when they came to court and the court declares the pledge in his possession; and likewise if they came to court and established the pledge in his hand, none disagree it is his and he transgresses. However, our case deals in an unspecified manner when the time expired some days before Pesach and until they ceased borrowing and lending in this and finished the matter between them, or in court, Pesach days arrived — certainly by itself the pledge is not acquired by him because of his acquisition, for from the outset since it was asmakhta and now he certainly does not want this right to vindicate him by their law and it becomes forbidden in benefit and he loses his debt. And likewise I found in Peri Megadim who wrote explicitly as our words that this law also depends on the dispute of Raavad and Shulchan Aruch.
chatam-sofer/1:_: In Magen Avraham s.k. 2 in s.v. veda etc., as stated in Chullin chapter 11 — the reference pei alef was deleted and should read pei yod, daf 131a.
chok-yaakov/1:א: That he lent a Jew on his chametz. Taz ruled nevertheless l'chatchila it is forbidden to lend a non-Jew on his chametz to redeem it after Pesach, for on Pesach he in any case transgresses bal yeira'eh; and it appears to me nevertheless, if at the time bi'ur arrived he said he would not redeem it again, he does not transgress and there is no prohibition at all, and likewise is the implication of the Gemara and the conclusion of Bach; and even concern of evasion is not applicable here as in siman 448 where we are concerned lest he evade and say he nullified even though he did not nullify — for there he does so not to forbid and lose his chametz b'dieved, unlike here where b'dieved there is certainly no prohibition and loss, since he does not redeem the chametz; in truth it is acquired by the non-Jew retroactively, and the end proves the beginning that he did not intend to redeem again once bi'ur time arrived — why should he redeem, since it is forbidden to him?
chok-yaakov/1:ב: He pledged it in his hand and said to him from now. But if he did not say to him from now, even though he left it as pledge with him, a non-Jew from a Jew does not acquire a pledge; and likewise where he said from now and did not leave it as pledge, even though the time is before Pesach, nevertheless since it is in the Jew's hand it is on his responsibility and is no worse than a non-Jew who deposited his chametz with a Jew on the Jew's responsibility, who is obligated to destroy, as above siman 440 — all this is explained in the Gemara and poskim, and this is also the view of Rosh and Raavad, except that he challenged Rambam for requiring from now; and their view is that if the time arrived before Pesach, even without from now the chametz is permitted since there is no asmakhta with a non-Jew; but leaving it as pledge with him is nevertheless required, and likewise implied somewhat in the Gemara in chapter Kol Sha'ah on that which the Gemara challenges Rava who said Bach from here and onward he collects from the Mishnah of a non-Jew who lent a Jew on his chametz that it is permitted after Pesach — implying he collects retroactively; and they establish that Mishnah when he left it as pledge with him, and do not establish that Mishnah even without leaving it as pledge when the time arrived before Pesach, and he would not need to establish that Mishnah also where he said from now, per Rosh and Raavad — and likewise explained explicitly in Rosh's words in what he presses to establish Tosafot there and does not establish when he did not leave it as pledge with him; therefore we require the time arrived before Pesach — but certainly when the time arrived before Pesach, nevertheless we require he left it as pledge with him. And do not answer me from that which Rosh explained in Nedarim daf 86 that chametz removes from the lien, and Rosh explained there: a Jew who made his chametz collateral to a non-Jew that if he does not redeem it by a set time after Pesach it shall be his — the time passed and he did not pay, it is forbidden in benefit because it was in the Jew's possession until redemption time, and the prohibition of chametz removed the non-Jew's lien; therefore it implies specifically when he set a time after Pesach, but before Pesach it does not remove the non-Jew's lien (although there it deals without leaving as pledge, only collateral, and likewise Ran wrote explicitly there, and likewise Rashi in Ketubot daf 59). One can say: although it does not remove the non-Jew's lien literally, since it belongs to the non-Jew before Pesach, nevertheless the obligation to destroy applies because it is under his hand and responsibility — and all this is clear and simple for one who examines their words well, not like Bach who explained Rosh and Raavad's words in seif 2 differently. And the acharonim wrote in the name of Shach: if they transferred it to the non-Jew through his kinyan or via land, even though they did not deliver it to the non-Jew until after Pesach, it is permitted provided it is not on the Jew's responsibility — end quote. And how is the non-Jew's kinyan effected? See Choshen Mishpat siman 123 and acharonim there, and above siman 448.
chok-yaakov/1:ג: And said to him from now. Beit Yosef's view per Magen Avraham's explanation: thus agreed most poskim that everything depends on from now, whether the time arrived before Pesach or after Pesach; if he did not say from now the chametz is forbidden, and if he said from now it is effective and is not asmakhta, since he said from now — for what is effective regarding a pledge, if it were not a pledge from now would not be effective to remove asmakhta, as explained in Choshen Mishpat siman 207 in Semag; and likewise Magen Avraham.
chok-yaakov/1:ד: From now it shall be yours. Magen Avraham wrote: requires study whether if he did not say from now the chametz is forbidden if he is obligated to redeem it from the non-Jew; and he wrote several more disputes on this; and see what is written in siman 440 s.k. 4; and one should be stringent and redeem it, since chametz removes from the lien — he ends up paying his debt from prohibited benefit.
chok-yaakov/1:ה: And the time arrived and he did not pay, it is permitted — and we do not say since it is in his hand to redeem he transgresses on Pesach because of bal yeira'eh, since he lacks money we do not say since; and likewise Ran in chapter Elu Overin; and further in my humble opinion: since the time of prohibition passed and it became forbidden, if he redeems we do not say since, for he certainly will not redeem in order to forbid the chametz and cause loss — and likewise Tosafot divide in chapter Elu Overin (Pesachim daf 46b) s.v. he'eil vekamushel above s.k. 5 this reasoning — see there.
chok-yaakov/2:א: If he pledged it in his hand. Rosh Yosef challenged per Rosh and R' Yonah that I brought above siman 440 s.k. 14: a Jew who deposited his chametz with a non-Jew even though the non-Jew accepted liability, nevertheless it is forbidden — if so, even though the chametz is in the non-Jew's hand it is forbidden since the Jew acquired it retroactively, it is like deposit with a non-Jew — end quote. And in my humble opinion the dispute is: nevertheless they needed to say he pledged it in his hand, for otherwise even in an actual sale we do not say money acquires from a non-Jew — see Choshen Mishpat siman 134 and Shach there s.k. 1. And further one can say: even for that view that money acquires in general, here it is only through asmakhta and he does not rely on the non-Jew; even with from now it is not effective unless he pledged it in his hand — see Choshen Mishpat siman 73 seif 17, and likewise there s.k. 3.
chok-yaakov/2:ב: Because he acquired it retroactively. And automatically he transgressed bal yeira'eh and bal yimatzei; therefore nullification and destruction are required like his chametz, and such is the implication of the poskim and Bach; and not like Magen Avraham who wrote that on Pesach the Jew is not obligated to destroy; and in Be'er Heitev he wrote that nullification alone suffices — I do not know whence these leniencies came to them.
chok-yaakov/2:ג: And he is not liable for it. And in an unspecified pledge from a non-Jew there is no liability on the Jew, as written above end of siman 440; and see Tosafot beginning of Kiddushin daf 8b and Gittin daf 37 s.v. she'ani mishkon — these laws are explained: there is no difference whether he pledged at the time of the loan or not at the time of the loan — see there.
chok-yaakov/2:ד: Permitted. Because a Jew from a non-Jew does not acquire a pledge; and see below siman 443 regarding a Jew's pledge.
chokhmat-shlomo/1:_: Seif 1: a non-Jew who lent a Jew on his chametz, etc. Nemukei Yosef: see what is written on this in the responsum to Rabbi [so-and-so] Nadvarna on what he challenged regarding Rambam that we require his time arrived before Pesach — he acquires from its place, as inserted in Hilchot Nedarim siman 221 incidentally — see there in my writings still in manuscript; examine. And see in Magen Avraham s.k. 2 what he brought of Raavad's view that there is no asmakhta with a non-Jew; and see in my writings to Choshen Mishpat edition 4 siman 47 what proof he brought for this from Gittin daf 43b — see there and examine. And see in Magen Avraham s.k. 3 what he wrote that one must tithe because it is like one compelled by the king, etc.; and see in my writings on Choshen Mishpat siman 443 and in my indexes to Shulchan Aruch it is in siman 486 — what he wrote that this is not comparable to that — see there. And in my writings to Hilchot Pesach I elaborated greatly on this — see there, with God's help; examine. And behold we read like the Yerushalmi in chapter 2 of Pesachim halachah 2: there we taught: a slave whom his master made collateral, etc. R' Chagai stood before R' Yosi: the Mishnah disagrees with R' Yishmael — a Jew who lent a non-Jew on his chametz, after Pesach permitted in benefit, etc. And see in Kaf HaChayim in Shirrei Korban who challenged from the baraita to support from the Mishnah that we taught: a Jew who lent a gentile on his chametz, after Pesach forbidden in benefit — see there, for the text was corrupted that it deals with from now, and that is forced, for in every such case he should have specified. But it appears more likely that the Mishnah deals after Pesach when his intent is to leave it in the lender's hand; therefore stringently we say retroactive declaration and it was clarified that also on Pesach it was in the Jew's possession and therefore forbidden; and conversely regarding a gentile who lent a Jew and his intent afterward to leave it — therefore permitted in benefit. But the baraita deals when his intent is not to leave it — therefore permitted in benefit. But the baraita of a slave whom his master made collateral deals explicitly when his intent is not to leave, since he said both can release — proven his intent is not to leave; therefore he properly challenges from that Mishnah that also deals when his intent is not to leave, and it comes out well, with God's help; examine.
dagul-merevavah/1:_: And see there in Shach s.k. 30 who holds chalipin are not effective, and requires study regarding a non-Jew.
dagul-merevavah/2:_: And in Rashi and in Pesachim daf 31b s.v. higa'aticha it does not imply so.
eliyah-rabbah/1:_: [1] And he pledged it in his hand, etc. And if he said to him from now and transferred through kinyan or land, even though he did not deliver it to the non-Jew's hand, it is permitted provided it is not on the Jew's responsibility (Shaltai Gibborim); and see Choshen Mishpat siman 195 seif 14 that one must acquire through the non-Jew's sudar.
eliyah-rabbah/2:_: [2] Permitted, etc. It appears that if his intent is that he will not redeem it by the time set after Pesach, it is permitted l'chatchila to lend on it in this manner, as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 120 seif 11 regarding immersing vessels; but to lend in an unspecified manner in this way is forbidden l'chatchila. And if he set a time before Pesach and did not redeem it, it is obvious it is permitted; and even if he redeemed after Pesach it is like a new acquisition. Chok Yaakov wrote: if at the time bi'ur arrived he said he would not redeem it, he does not transgress at all.
eshel-avraham/1:א: In his hand. Specifically, for we hold like Bach that from here and onward he collects — meaning we do not consider it retroactively as if it were the non-Jew's on Pesach.
eshel-avraham/1:ב: Belonging to the non-Jew. And he said to him: since it is in his hand to redeem, he shall transgress on it, as written regarding challah: since he lacks money we do not say since. And Chayei Adam explained: how could he redeem it and it would be forbidden in benefit? And see Tosafot Pesachim 42b. And Taz raised: if his intent is to redeem after Pesach it is forbidden, for it is like hiding; and Magen Avraham challenged: is it not that when the pledge is compelled he must pay the loan value and it will be forbidden? And one can explain: in any case it is no worse than one who accepts liability for a non-Jew's chametz in a non-Jew's house — permitted, as written Choshen Mishpat siman 207.
eshel-avraham/2:_: Permitted. In Rosh Yosef he challenged from siman 440: a Jew who deposited with a non-Jew with liability etc. — Chayei Adam explained: certainly when there is no pledge in his hand it is nothing, for even in renting money one does not acquire from a non-Jew — Choshen Mishpat siman 154. And even if they acquired, nevertheless here it is only asmakhta and is not effective without a pledge in his hand; and he had no view regarding immersing vessels because in any case it appears as his; and see Yoreh De'ah siman 120. And know: also if his intent is to leave it with him he does not transgress as long as he did not sell it to him explicitly — Magen Avraham; and see Choshen Mishpat siman 73 — many laws and disputes regarding pledge.
kaf-hachayyim/1:_: (1) [Seif 1] A non-Jew who lent a Jew on his chametz, etc. L'chatchila it is forbidden to lend a non-Jew on his chametz to redeem it after Pesach, for it is like hiding in the non-Jew's hand and he transgresses bal yeira'eh; but if he intended to redeem before Pesach and afterward it continued that he does not redeem before Pesach, he is not obligated to destroy, for if he does not redeem before Pesach he cannot redeem after Pesach, for then it will be forbidden — Taz s.k. 2. Chok Yosef vol. 1: and it appears from his words that if in his mind he will not redeem at all even after Pesach, it is permitted l'chatchila since he set a time and said from now; and likewise R' Akiva Eiger vol. 2, and likewise Peri Chadash that it is permitted even l'chatchila on condition that when the time arrives he will finalize in his mind not to redeem further — see there. And likewise Chayei Adam vol. 1: if at bi'ur time he said to the non-Jew he will not redeem again, he does not transgress and there is no prohibition at all — see there. And they brought R' Akiva Eiger there. Mekor Chayim vol. 1: however Chayei Adam general rule 128 end of vol. 7 wrote one should be stringent and redeem before Pesach.
kaf-hachayyim/2:_: (2) There. And he pledged it in his hand. But if he did not pledge it in the non-Jew's hand, only the non-Jew lent him on it and the chametz still rests in the Jew's possession — although he said to him from now, it is no worse than a non-Jew's chametz in the Jew's possession with liability on the Jew, which is forbidden — Rosh, Taz s.k. 1, Magen Avraham s.k. 1. And if he said to him from now and transferred it to the non-Jew through kinyan or via land, even though they did not deliver it to the non-Jew until after Pesach, it is permitted provided it was not on the Jew's responsibility all the days of Pesach — Riaz and Beit Yosef in Shach chapter Kol Sha'ah, Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Tur, Magen Avraham there. And he wrote there Magen Avraham that one must acquire through the non-Jew's sudar as written in Choshen Mishpat siman 123 seif 4. However Shach there s.k. 30 wrote chalipin and sudar-kinyan with a non-Jew are not effective except only with money or pulling per one opinion and per another — see there; and Nekudat HaKesef agreed to his words in this note 1; and see below note 9.
machatzit-hashekel/1:א: (s.k. 1) And he pledged it etc. — it is no worse etc. in the Jew's possession. Meaning the liability is on the Jew, and the Jew transgresses as written siman 440.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ב: And in Shach he wrote etc. through kinyan — meaning sudar-kinyan. And know Shach does not disagree with Rosh; both intended the same thing. Only Rosh left his words unspecified, and Shach explained the matter more, as known from the dispute of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam: Rashi ruled like R' Yochanan that with a Jew pulling acquires from the Torah; if so, with a gentile money acquires and not pulling. Rabbeinu Tam ruled like R' Yehudah that with a Jew money acquires from the Torah; therefore with a gentile specifically pulling is required. Rosh holds like Rabbeinu Tam that with a gentile specifically pulling is required. If so, that which Rosh wrote: but if he did not pledge it etc. — it is no worse than a gentile's chametz in a Jew's possession that is forbidden — implies the prohibition is only because liability is on the Jew; meaning he said to him from now, and if so if he did not pay after Pesach the matter is revealed retroactively that from the time of the loan it belonged to the gentile, and it is like selling it to the gentile at the time of the loan — nevertheless with what did he acquire, since he did not pledge it with the gentile and did not pull? There is only giving money, which does not acquire from a gentile per Rosh; therefore it deals when he acquired through sudar-kinyan or via land, only Rosh left it unspecified and did not speak of kinyan; and even if he acquired, he wrote nevertheless it is forbidden because liability is on the Jew; therefore Shach wrote: if the gentile acquired through sudar-kinyan or via land and liability is on the gentile it is permitted; but if the gentile did not acquire, even though liability is on the gentile, nevertheless it is forbidden, as written end of siman 440.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ג: And in Choshen Mishpat etc. in the gentile's sudar — for we hold like Rav that the kinyan shall be in the sudar of the acquirer; however the custom is that since the majority there are witnesses at the time of kinyan who will not deny one of them in the kinyan, therefore they acquire in the witnesses' sudar; and for this reason the witnesses write in the document and kinyan from so-and-so etc., meaning they acquired from so-and-so — and that is through the acquirer's agency, for one may benefit a person not in his presence, for presumably it pleases him that he be his agent and acquire on his behalf. Not so with a gentile, since we hold there is no agency for a gentile and he cannot appoint an agent; therefore one cannot acquire through the witnesses' sudar, only in the gentile's sudar himself. However Shach there doubted the essence of the law — namely Rabbeinu Tam holds a gentile also acquires through chalipin, but Shach was compelled that there is no law of chalipin with a gentile; and he wrote thus in responsum of Maharam Mintz and responsum of Maharashdam — see there.
machatzit-hashekel/2:א: And he said to him from now etc. — there is no law of asmakhta with a gentile. Meaning: in chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechirah Rambam and Raavad disagree. Rambam's view: in a matter the acquirer is holding, there is no asmakhta; therefore he wrote: the acquirer acquires a thing from his fellow and the acquirer gave the seller a deposit and said to him: if I retract, my deposit is forgiven you; and the seller says: if I retract I will double your deposit for you (meaning I will pay you double the deposit) — if the seller retracts he need not double his deposit, for it is asmakhta; but if the acquirer retracts, the seller acquired the deposit since the seller holds the deposit. Raavad disagrees and holds even what is in the acquirer's hand has asmakhta; if so, here where he said if I do not redeem by a set time it shall be yours, it is asmakhta; namely with from now asmakhta is removed, as written in Choshen Mishpat siman 207, since he said he should acquire from now — we see he transfers to him wholeheartedly and his intent is only to rely on complete acquisition; nevertheless where he did not say from now, per Raavad even in a pledge in a gentile's hand there is asmakhta, and therefore he said there is no asmakhta. And a gentile acquires in every matter.
machatzit-hashekel/2:ב: Everything depends on from now. Meaning: even if the time arrived before Pesach, nevertheless from now is required, for otherwise it is asmakhta; even per Rambam who holds where it is in his hand we do not say asmakhta — nevertheless with a gentile in every matter his acquisition is weak and it is asmakhta even if it is in the gentile's hand; therefore from now is required to remove asmakhta. And such is Rav Yosef Karo's view in Shulchan Aruch that wrote even if the time he set did not arrive until after Pesach — implying not only when the time arrived before Pesach is the law so, but even when the time arrived after Pesach the law is likewise, for such is the nature of the language everywhere; and likewise Rav Yosef Karo. Behold also when the time arrived before Pesach he holds from now is required, for specifically in a pledge from now is effective. For in siman 297 seif 9 he wrote: he lent him on a field worth a hundred gold and it is worth more, and said to him: if you do not pay me within three years it shall be mine — it is asmakhta; but if he said: if you do not pay me within three years it shall be mine from now, it is not asmakhta — it is clear from now asmakhta is removed; and in seif 14 Rama wrote: and some say from now alone is insufficient to remove asmakhta unless he acquires from him in an important court and from now; and in seif 9 Rama did not emend — implying he agrees. Therefore Semag wrote s.k. 18, and such is his language: this case is different (in a pledge), for they gave it to his hand immediately as a pledge and lien on his money, and it is like a sale; and also he did him a favor by lending him; therefore we say his intent is it should be his from then, a complete acquisition, only he conditioned it should be in his hand to redeem within three years — end quote Semag; if so, the same here without lending him money, only he said to him: if I do not do for you etc., even if the time arrived before Pesach it is forbidden, for it is asmakhta per the view Rama brought in Choshen Mishpat unless he acquired in an important court.
machatzit-hashekel/2:ג: And see what is written siman 440 seif 1: we do not follow their law. For he wrote there in Shulchan Aruch: even if he is not liable for it by law, only the gentile was compelled etc., he is obligated to destroy it; and some disagree, and their dispute depends on the Gemara sugya where Rava said to the people of Mechoza: in your city chametz of soldiers is forbidden, since these steal or lose and you will need to pay etc.; and Rambam holds there was no obligation from the law, only from compulsion, and nevertheless Rava said they must destroy. Raavad holds where the obligation is only from compulsion, destruction is not required, only where it was from the law and royal decree — see there. And what is written siman 448 seif 1 that he brought Mishna Berurah's view that we follow their law regarding acquisition, and Magen Avraham holds we do not follow their law — see there. But in truth one can distinguish between the law of asmakhta explained in this siman and the law of acquisition explained in siman 448, as Magen Avraham wrote in siman 448.
magen-avraham/1:א: And he pledged it in his hand. But if he did not pledge it in the non-Jew's hand, only the non-Jew lent him on it and the chametz still rests in the Jew's possession — although he said to him from now, it is no worse than a non-Jew's chametz in the Jew's possession with liability on the Jew, which is forbidden (Rosh). And in Shach he wrote: if they transferred it to the non-Jew through kinyan or via land, even though they did not deliver it to the non-Jew until after Pesach, it is permitted provided it is not on the Jew's responsibility — end quote. And in Choshen Mishpat siman 123 seif 4 one must acquire through the non-Jew's sudar.
magen-avraham/1:ב: And said to him from now. And if the time arrived before Pesach, even if he did not say to him from now he acquired it, for there is no law of asmakhta with a non-Jew (Raavad); and Magen Avraham wrote that most acharonim hold everything depends on from now, and so appears from the halachot and Rabbeinu Yehudah and R' Yehudah ibn Gayat, and such is primary — end quote; and such is Rav Yosef Karo's view in Shulchan Aruch. And if he did not lend him on it, only said to him: if I do not do for you a certain matter before Rosh Chodesh Nisan the chametz shall be yours from now — it is forbidden, for it is asmakhta, as written in Choshen Mishpat siman 207 in Semag that specifically in a pledge from now is effective; and see what we wrote siman 448 seif 3 whether we follow their law.
magen-avraham/1:ג: And he did not pay, it is permitted. And it is difficult: let us say since it is in his hand to redeem on Pesach he transgresses, as we say regarding challah — since if he wishes he can remove the liability; and one can say: here, since he lacks money we do not say since (Ran); and Bach was in doubt whether it is permitted l'chatchila to lend a non-Jew in this manner — this explanation applies only b'dieved. Difficulty: even if he left it in the non-Jew's hand, nevertheless if the pledge is compelled the Jew would have to pay, as stated in Choshen Mishpat siman 72 — if so, it is in the Jew's possession; and one can say: it is like one who accepts liability for a non-Jew's chametz in the non-Jew's house, which is permitted as written siman 440; or we judge him by their law as we wrote. And know: if one of these matters is lacking that we said is forbidden — meaning it is forbidden for any Jew to derive benefit from that chametz even though it is in the non-Jew's hand; and requires study whether if he did not say to him from now he is obligated to redeem it from the non-Jew and destroy it, for otherwise he pays his debt from prohibited benefit, and it is like one whom the king compelled regarding his threshing floor in payment of a debt that he must tithe, as stated in Chullin chapter 11. And if it is still in the Jew's hand only that he pledged it to the non-Jew, it is obvious it is forbidden to give it to him. But if he did not lend him on it, only gave it to the non-Jew as a gift, such as if he said to him: if I do not do this thing for you on a certain day the chametz shall be yours from now as we wrote — he need not give its value to the non-Jew and destroy it, for even if you say the non-Jew did not acquire, nevertheless the Jew does not remove anything from it; but if it is in the Jew's hand it is forbidden to give it to him, for it is forbidden in benefit and forbidden to give to others.
magen-avraham/2:א: He is not liable for it, forbidden. It appears to me that on Pesach the Jew is not obligated to destroy it, for it is still in the non-Jew's possession since perhaps he will redeem it; and even if the non-Jew came on Pesach and gave its value, it is permitted to let the non-Jew take it, as written siman 440.
magen-avraham/2:ב: Because he acquired it for him. If so, even if he did not pledge it in his hand, if he transferred it to him with from now it is forbidden, as we wrote.
magen-avraham/2:ג: But if he did not say to him etc., permitted. For we hold a Jew from a non-Jew and a non-Jew from a Jew do not acquire a pledge (Rosh). And he had a view regarding what is written in Yoreh De'ah siman 120 seif 9 regarding immersing vessels that it is a doubt, for there the reason is because it appears as his; and in Choshen Mishpat siman 253 end of Hagahah: it appears to me that even though it appears from the non-Jew's intent that he intends it to remain in his possession, nevertheless he does not transgress as long as he did not sell it to him explicitly; and in Choshen Mishpat siman 73 — and from this it implies a Jew who takes a pledge from his fellow who lent him transgresses, for a Jew from a Jew acquires a pledge; and see what we wrote siman 443.
mechaber/1:main: The law of one who lent on chametz. Contains 2 seifim. A non-Jew who lent a Jew on his chametz and pledged it in his (the non-Jew's) hand, and said to him: from now it shall be yours if I do not repay you by a set time, and the time arrived and he did not repay him — it is permitted, even if the time he set did not arrive until after Pesach; for when the time arrived and he did not repay him, it is acquired by him retroactively, and it is his chametz belonging to the non-Jew.
mechaber/2:main: A Jew who lent a non-Jew on his chametz — if he pledged it in his (the Jew's) hand and said to him from now, and the time arrived even after Pesach and he did not repay him, even if he is not liable for it — it is forbidden, because the Jew acquires it retroactively. But if he did not say to him from now, and he is not liable for it — it is permitted.
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (1) From now it shall be yours — meaning he said to him: acquire for yourself from now if [I do not repay] etc., and not merely as a general lien on the pledge.
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (2) And the time arrived and he did not pay him, etc. — and the reason is: since when the time arrived and he did not pay, it is acquired by him retroactively and it is the non-Jew's chametz over which Pesach passed, and it is permitted even for eating; therefore we require that he say to him from now, and also that the chametz be tevoi yadai — for if he did not say to him from now, behold on Pesach the chametz was the Jew's, only that afterward from when the time arrived and onward it was acquired by the non-Jew and is forbidden even in benefit to every Jew; and likewise if the chametz was not tevoi yadai, the chametz was not acquired for him at all even through from now, for with what did he acquire — behold he did not pull it to himself. However, if he transferred the chametz to the non-Jew through kinyan and from now if he will not pay by a set time, several acharonim hold that in this case even if the pledge remained tevoi yadai of the Jew it is permitted if the Jew conditioned that he does not accept liability for the pledge; and some are stringent on this — see Biur Halachah.
mishnah-berurah/1:ג: (3) Permitted — meaning the chametz is permitted to derive sustenance from it; nevertheless l'chatchila the poskim were in doubt whether it is permitted for a Jew to lend in this manner even in his heart not to redeem it, since it is in his hand to redeem on Pesach — therefore perhaps he nevertheless transgresses; therefore one should be stringent and redeem before Pesach; and all the more so when at the time of the loan he intends to redeem after Pesach — certainly forbidden, for it is like hiding in his hand [Taz]; and Chayei Adam wrote: if at bi'ur time he said to the non-Jew he will not redeem again, there is no prohibition.
mishnah-berurah/1:ד: (4) Even if the time did not arrive etc. — meaning: even though during Pesach the matter was in doubt lest he redeem it, nevertheless we do not forbid because of this after Pesach, as he concludes when the time arrived etc. And it appears from the Mechaber's view who wrote even that likewise if the time arrived before Pesach and he did not redeem, it is also not permitted unless he said to him at the time he pledged the chametz in his hand that it shall be his from now if he does not redeem it; and the reason is: without from now the gentile did not acquire his pledge even when the time they set arrived and he did not redeem, because it is mere asmakhta, and automatically the chametz is the Jew's and forbidden even after Pesach because of chametz over which Pesach passed; and likewise several acharonim. And some are lenient on this, and one may rely on them in a time of need; and all this is only regarding forbidding the chametz if Pesach already passed; but if it is still before Pesach, which is a d'oraisa concern, certainly one should be concerned for the stringent view that it is only asmakhta, and therefore he should appear to declare it to the non-Jew at the time bi'ur arrives.
mishnah-berurah/1:ה: (5) For when the time arrived and he did not pay him etc. — and the acharonim wrote that from now being effective is specifically like in our case where he lent him money and the chametz was as a pledge, and in this we say from now is effective [for he certainly agreed to transfer to him in truth, since he did him a favor and lent him]; but without a loan, only a general condition, such as if he gave him his chametz and said to him: if I do not do for you a certain matter before Pesach the chametz shall be yours — and he did not fulfill the condition — even if he said to him from now, it is also asmakhta for many poskim [unless he transferred in an important court, as explained in Choshen Mishpat siman 207 seif 14 in Hagahah], and the chametz is still the Jew's and he must give the chametz to the non-Jew as a complete gift before Pesach; however b'dieved if Pesach passed, it appears we need not be stringent to forbid the chametz.
mishnah-berurah/1:ו: (6) Retroactively — before Pesach, because he said from now, as above; and Magen Avraham was in doubt where he did not say to him from now whether the chametz is forbidden forever if he is obligated to redeem it from the non-Jew after Pesach and destroy it, for otherwise behold he benefits by paying his debt to the non-Jew from prohibited benefit; and in Beit Meir and Sefer Mekor Chayim they agreed to permit, for behold he does not pay his debt with his hands — only it remained in the non-Jew's hand by itself, and what the non-Jew does not claim him for this benefit is automatically not our concern; however with chametz in the Jew's hand that he pledged to the gentile and Pesach passed, it is forbidden in benefit, and likewise in this it is obvious it is forbidden to give it to the non-Jew, for this benefit itself.
mishnah-berurah/2:א: (7) In his hand — for otherwise the pledge is not acquired for him, for he did not pull; unless he transferred it to the Jew through a valid kinyan and from now, as above in Mishna Berurah s.k. 1.
mishnah-berurah/2:ב: (8) Forbidden — for it is chametz of a Jew over which Pesach passed, forbidden in benefit because he transgressed bal yeira'eh. And know the Mechaber stated its law regarding prohibition of the chametz after Pesach, and the same applies before Pesach regarding bal yeira'eh that he is obligated to destroy it or sell this chametz at the time of selling like his other chametz, lest the non-Jew not redeem when the time arrives as they set, and it turns out retroactively the chametz was his and he transgresses bal yeira'eh; and see Biur Halachah. And if he transgressed and did not destroy it and the non-Jew came during Pesach to redeem it, he may accept money from him and let him take his chametz [acharonim].
mishnah-berurah/2:ג: (9) But if he did not say to him etc. — for we hold a Jew from a gentile and a gentile from a Jew do not acquire a pledge; it turns out it was not in his possession until after Pesach. And it appears from the Mechaber's view that likewise for its entire time before Pesach, if he did not pay, the chametz is also permitted after Pesach if he did not say to him from now, for asmakhta does not acquire; and we already wrote above some disagree that this is not asmakhta, and per that view it becomes chametz of a Jew and he must sell it before Pesach or destroy it; and one should be careful in this, for many stand on this view. However if Pesach passed, perhaps one may rely on the Mechaber's view here and it is permitted, as above in seif 1.
mishnah-berurah/2:ד: (10) And he is not liable for it — for if he were liable for it, it would in any case be forbidden, for it is no worse than if the non-Jew's chametz were deposited with him with liability, in which case he transgresses, as above siman 440.
mishnah-berurah/2:ה: (11) Permitted — and even if it appears from the non-Jew's intent that he intends it to remain in his (the Jew's) possession, nevertheless he does not transgress as long as he did not sell it to him explicitly; and this is when the pledge is between a Jew and a non-Jew. But a Jew who takes a pledge from his fellow Jew who lent him — even without from now, the lender acquires the pledge and he transgresses, for a Jew acquires a pledge from his fellow Jew; and see above at the end of siman 440 that the borrower also transgresses since the chametz itself is his.
netiv-chayim/1:_: (Magen Avraham s.k. 1) And in Shach he wrote. Nemukei Yosef: And I say the Rosh also agrees that kinyan is effective, and I elaborated on this not like Bach.
netiv-chayim/2:_: (s.k. 6) He does not acquire a pledge. Nemukei Yosef: Nevertheless one must condition that there is no liability on him — meaning he conditioned explicitly that even if the pledge is lost; for if he did not condition explicitly, even though he did not acquire a pledge by Torah law, nevertheless it is called double payment on him because of that which Shmuel [said]: a lost sack that rolls away — a lost thousand zuz, even though Shmuel deals when he specified — nevertheless regarding a pledge it is like specification, as Tosafot wrote in chapter HaUmanin 2 s.v. lo etc. — see there.
peri-megadim/1:_: And he pledged it. Taz: it appears to emend and thus read from now, for otherwise Bach in an unspecified case does not acquire retroactively per Rava, and therefore we require from now; and the words that it is not etc. have no explanation; and we also require leaving as pledge, for otherwise liability is on the Jew — Rosh Pesachim 41. And it is possible to reconcile the text from what implies in Pesachim for Abaye one need not leave as pledge — see there Maharsha and Gittin 40:1 in Rashi s.v. chametz and Penei Yehoshua there. And at first glance one would say for Abaye without leaving as pledge he collects retroactively, and a non-Jew acquires a pledge through money per R' Yochanan — see Tosafot Kiddushin 14b s.v. he'eil per Rashi's explanation; and for Rava he establishes per the halachah like R' Yochanan that a non-Jew acquires only through pulling — and with what will he acquire? Therefore specifically when left as pledge (and see Magen Avraham 1 in the name of Shach, and it will be explained there). And it is possible for Abaye without leaving as pledge, and even a non-Jew from a Jew acquires retroactively, for lien of debt is stronger than acquisition through money — know that money alone even with a Jew does not acquire by rabbinic law, and nevertheless if one consecrated, the lender cannot retract — and why, since by rabbinic law he did not acquire, is it not his, analogous to one who consecrated chametz on the sixth? And even if you say this — nevertheless it is difficult; rather we strengthen lien of debt more than acquisition through money; if so for Abaye money-kinyan is not required. And that which Taz wrote the Rosh meant Rava need not etc., and he transferred to him through kinyan — nevertheless forbidden because liability is on the Jew; and with a condition that there is no liability on him, and through kinyan it is permitted b'dieved even without leaving as pledge, as Magen Avraham wrote in the name of Shach — thus one can explain Taz's words. And such is Taz's language: the pledge must be in his hand, for we hold like Rava and from now a non-Jew does not acquire a pledge — and this teaches as we wrote that for Abaye one need not leave as pledge; and if a non-Jew acquires a pledge the borrower does not transgress, as Magen Avraham note 6 wrote, and it will be explained there; also in Taz Magen Avraham note 3 disagrees on this — see there. I again examined in Milchamot: he wrote for Abaye in the conclusion also leaving as pledge is required; and that which one consecrated and the lender sold — for Abaye consecration applies in real property that he acquired through document, not in movable property — see there he elaborated, and it will be explained further in Magen Avraham.
peri-megadim/2:_: Permitted. Taz: behold the dispute of Rosh and Raavad with Rabbeinu Efraim and Rambam is explained well in Magen Avraham chapter 4 of Choshen Mishpat, and I will explain briefly: behold Rambam and Rabbeinu Efraim — all three conditions: left as pledge, did not redeem, and from now we require specifically before Pesach; after Pesach from now is not effective, since for stringency and it is in his hand to redeem (and of Heaven's property one who does not transgress must distinguish — see Tosafot Pesachim 46b s.v. he'eil 2). And before Pesach three conditions: first, without from now the non-Jew does not acquire; and although Rabbeinu Efraim from Mechirah holds asmakhta does not apply to a pledge, a non-Jew is weaker still; and likewise without leaving as pledge — with what will he acquire? Or because of liability; and likewise if he transferred through kinyan to a minor and without liability, one need not leave as pledge; and see Magen Avraham 2, explained for us not to rush without leaving as pledge. And Rosh and Raavad's view: those three conditions apply when the time arrived after Pesach and it is effective; before Pesach two suffice: he did not redeem and left as pledge, even if he did not say from now, for there is no asmakhta with a non-Jew; and leaving as pledge is required — with what will he acquire? Or because of liability; and where he transferred through kinyan and conditioned there is no liability on him, it is permitted when the time arrived before Pesach without leaving as pledge and without from now. And from Taz's conclusion it appears the Mechaber also holds that before Pesach without from now it is permitted; and the word even explains not entirely equating them; and likewise above; and see Levush and Magen Avraham note 2 did not explain so. And Taz ruled: if he intends thus it is forbidden; and if he lent him and bi'ur time arrived and he did not redeem, we do not compel him to redeem — implying l'chatchila in any case it is forbidden to borrow from the non-Jew on such a condition lest he redeem; and even if he finalizes in his mind not to redeem, nevertheless l'chatchila it is forbidden because of since it is in his hand to redeem; and although b'dieved it is permitted because he lacks money it is not considered since, as Ran wrote, or how could he redeem since it is forbidden in benefit — but l'chatchila forbidden and inexpensive. And in R' Akiva Eiger note 2: even l'chatchila one may lend in this manner if his intent is not to redeem after Pesach — see there.
rabbi-akiva-eiger/1:_: (Magen Avraham s.k. 2) Asmakhta with a non-Jew is not because kinyan by their law is effective, but since in their law they do not judge the law of asmakhta, he finalizes and acquires — so wrote Magen Avraham below siman 448 seif 4. In our matter I did not merit to understand: behold the foundation that asmakhta does not acquire — even though through the condition he should have acquired and he knows that if there will not be money this will acquire — nevertheless we say he thinks in his mind that certainly he will have money and it will not come to this that this will acquire, and he did not finalize and acquire; if so, what difference does it make that in their law they do not judge asmakhta — nevertheless they judge only that if he does not pay he will acquire, and he thinks in his mind he will pay and did not finalize and acquire; behold also in their law he should have acquired if he does not pay him, and nevertheless we say he did not finalize and acquire because he thinks clearly he will certainly pay — and what is the wonder in this that with a gentile they do not judge asmakhta, and if he does not pay this will acquire — nevertheless in his mind he will certainly pay and he did not finalize and acquire; requires study.
rabbi-akiva-eiger/2:_: (Magen Avraham s.k. 3) The Jew would have been obligated to pay — for although the gentile acquired the chametz retroactively, that is when he wishes to transfer it; the borrower penalized himself that if he does not pay the chametz will be acquired retroactively; but nevertheless the lender can say: I do not wish to acquire it, and can compel him to pay my debt, for the condition is not to the borrower's detriment but to the lender's detriment. And what Magen Avraham did not challenge further: if he is compelled, automatically the borrower will not wish to acquire it, and retroactively it becomes the Jew's chametz — and this too is not resolved in Magen Avraham's answer that it is gentile's chametz in a gentile's house; for behold it is Jew's chametz — meaning in truth on Pesach the Jew transgresses in doubt lest the borrower compel him to pay; but nevertheless now after Pesach the gentile agrees to receive the chametz for his debt, and the matter is revealed retroactively that the chametz was gentiles' and permitted in benefit; therefore Magen Avraham challenged only that although it was revealed it was gentile's chametz, nevertheless it was on the Jew's responsibility and forbidden after Pesach like chametz of a gentile deposited in a Jew's hand who accepted liability, which is forbidden after Pesach as Magen Avraham holds siman 440, and as Rambam wrote explicitly and as proven also from Rosh and Shulchan Aruch seif 1 that if he did not leave as pledge it is forbidden after Pesach because of liability [this is not like Chayei Adam]; and on this Magen Avraham properly answered that it is gentile's chametz in a gentile's house; for behold now that he did not compel him to pay, the matter is revealed that it is gentile's chametz; and per this reasoning what Magen Avraham wrote initially and Bach was in doubt whether permitted l'chatchila to lend a non-Jew etc. — at first glance there is no room for doubt, for certainly forbidden lest the gentile compel him to pay and it becomes Jew's chametz and he transgresses; examine. But per this reasoning there is a difficulty on seif 2: a Jew who lent etc. who acquires retroactively — behold the lender Jew can save his chametz and renounce its forbidden status by saying I do not wish to acquire it, and return the chametz to the gentile and compel him to pay; requires study.
turei-zahav/1:א: And he pledged it in his hand. For otherwise there is no permission, for Bach in an unspecified case collects from here and onward — meaning and we do not consider it retroactively as if it were the non-Jew's on Pesach; for he requires the Jew to say from now, for otherwise the non-Jew did not acquire for him and it stood in the Jew's possession and is forbidden. And likewise if he did not pledge it in his hand, although he said to him from now, it is no worse than a non-Jew's chametz in the Jew's possession with liability on the Jew — so wrote Rosh.
turei-zahav/1:ב: Permitted even if the time did not arrive etc. But if the time arrived before Pesach it is permitted even without from now, so Raavad and Rosh wrote, and not like Rabbeinu Efraim. And regarding permission to lend a non-Jew on his chametz l'chatchila — in my humble opinion: if at the time of the loan he intends to redeem it after Pesach, certainly forbidden to lend, for this is like hiding in the non-Jew's hand, as Rambam wrote chapter 4 of Torah law: leaven shall not be found in your houses, even if he hid it or deposited it with a non-Jew; and if he intended to redeem before Pesach and afterward it continued that he does not redeem before Pesach, it appears this is not within what is written end of siman 440 that one who deposits is obligated to destroy, as we explained there per Rambam and R' Yehudah — for there it is only a deposit, and whenever the Jew wishes he can take it, unlike here in a loan on it where there is no reason to say we compel him to redeem lest he wish to redeem after Pesach — why should we compel him to redeem? For if he does not redeem before Pesach he cannot redeem after Pesach, for then it will be forbidden, for retroactively it is his; if so, it is as though it was decided from today for the non-Jew in exchange for his money, as in my humble opinion.
turei-zahav/2:_: Even if he is not liable for it etc. In the Gemara they say: a non-Jew who left bread as pledge with a Jew does not transgress, and Rashi in Pesachim explained: he holds a Jew also does not acquire a pledge from a non-Jew; and if he said to him I have reached you, he transgresses — and we explain it that he said from now I have reached you; and Rashi explained: from now he says — if I do not repay you by a certain day I transgress; and even though the time did not arrive, perhaps when it arrives he will not pay and he ends up transgressing retroactively bal yeira'eh — end quote. And per this there is a difficulty on Tur who mentioned the law after Pesach and did not mention the law applicable on Pesach that he must destroy it if the non-Jew said from now, even though there is no liability on him; and it appears Tur included this in what he wrote that if liability is on the Jew, even in a mere deposit he must destroy — and that is during Pesach days; if so, it is a fortiori to what he wrote where the non-Jew said from now and even though there is no liability, he must destroy on Pesach, for there the doubt is in a matter that may become entirely his, and it is stricter than Jew's liability where there is no side that the chametz itself belongs to the Jew, as in my humble opinion.
yad-ephraim/1:_: See Taz s.k. 1: and he pledged it in his hand and said to him from now, for otherwise etc., as if it were the non-Jew's on Pesach; therefore he requires that he say etc. — thus read.
yad-ephraim/2:_: (there) In Magen Avraham s.k. 2: and so appears from the halachot and Baal HaItur and R' Yehudah ibn Gayat etc. — thus read.
